newsitem.title: GERMANY: Deutsche Telekom shares seen well below 30 marks. [CORRECTED 17:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Deutsche Telekom shares seen well below 30 marks. [CORRECTED 17:50 GMT]

text.p: Wheeling and dealing over the price for shares in Deutsche Telekom AG will turn white-hot next week when the company sets the price range for institutional investors in Europe's largest-ever flotation.

But despite overwhelming interest in the issue by private investors, fund managers and industry analysts say the risks are high and the share price will probably be well below the 30 mark target the company had hoped to gain.
When Telekom unveils its final sales prospectus on Monday, investors are expecting the company to set a range of 23 marks to 29 marks as it begins taking bids from investors on Tuesday.

"The fair value for us is around 23 marks to 24 marks, but that's likely to be the lower end of the range," Michael Makris, fund manager at Oppenheim Kapitalanlagen GmbH, said on Friday. "The initial offering price will probably be in the upper mid-20s."
Investors will have from October 22 until November 14 to place orders for some of the 500 million shares that Telekom will list on stock exchanges in Germany, New York and Tokyo.
The final price for the shares will be set during the weekend of November 16 and 17 and trade in the shares begins on November 18 in Europe and the United States and a day later in Japan.
Frank Rothauge, analyst with Helaba Trust, said he expected Telekom to announce a price range of either 24-28 marks or 25-29 marks and an initial share price of around 27 marks.
"The upper limit of the price range will be below 30 marks," he said.
A manager of a German pension fund who asked not to be named expected a price of between 26 marks and 27 marks.
"We are certainly going to take some of the shares. The closer the price is to 25 marks, the more we'll buy. At 27.50 marks to 28 marks it looks different," he said.

During bookbuilding Telekom will present itself to investors in so-called road shows. Investors will offer bids for Telekom shares, saying how many shares they would buy at which price within the range set on Monday.
Analysts from the banks managing Telekom's listing have varied in their estimates on a fair value for Telekom's shares.
According to press reports, Deutsche Bank and Dresdner Bank, two of the three banks leading the global listing, have been seeking a price range of 25 marks to 30 marks.

But U.S. investment bank Goldman Sachs, the other global coordinator, said in a report that using standard international evaluation methods for telecommunications companies, Telekom's share should cost between 20 marks and 25 marks, according to a report in Handelsblatt newspaper. (Corrects to add dropped reference sourcing statement to Handelsblatt.)

There are three main risks facing potential investors: Telekom's debt, threats to profitability when the telecoms sector is deregulated in 1998, and concern that shares will tumble next year after an initial steep rise this year.

Telekom is shouldering over 100 billion marks ($65 billion) in debt. It expects to be able to shave by one third in four years, but that depends on profitability, which could be dented by fierce competition after 1998.
Telekom's share price is expected surge at first.
On the basis of private investors alone, analysts expect Telekom's listing to be oversubscribed at least twofold.
Because Telekom and the German government have set preferences for private investors, there will be fewer shares for instituional investors in the initial offering.
These investors, large funds who will need to buy Telekom shares to be appropriately weighted in Germany, will be forced to buy stock on the open market, fuelling demand and driving up the price.
But when the party is over next year, the share price could fall back as concerns about its balance sheet take hold.
"We really expect the shares will rise sharply after the initial offering, but then the market could take revenge in 1997," said Rothauge.
